title: ShowerClear
question: How does a bathroom shower work?
hook: A shower makes no warm water of its own: it mixes two streams and throws the result through sixty tiny holes. See the mixing sum, the wax capsule and the sliding spool that stop it scalding you, and why a rain shower dribbles under an overhead tank.

explainer.title: Two pipes in, three ways out
explainer.text: Cold water comes down from the overhead tank, and a branch of it goes through the geyser. Hot and cold meet in the wall mixer, and a diverter sends the mix to the spout, the overhead head or the hand shower. A bend of water in the floor trap keeps sewer gas out.

explainer.title: Warm water is a sum
explainer.text: Outlet temperature = (hot flow × hot temperature + cold flow × cold temperature) ÷ total flow. Three litres a minute at 60 °C with five at 25 °C gives eight litres a minute at 38 °C. Open another cold tap and the cold pressure dips, so the mix jumps hotter.

explainer.title: A spool that balances pressure
explainer.text: A pressure-balancing valve has a piston that slides towards whichever side is weaker and pinches the stronger one. The pressures behind it stay equal, so the hot-to-cold share holds. The shower goes weaker for a moment, not hotter.

explainer.title: Wax that feels the water
explainer.text: A thermostatic valve keeps a capsule of wax in the mixed water. Warm wax swells and pushes a shuttle that narrows the hot gap and widens the cold one. If the cold supply fails, it shuts the hot off completely.

explainer.title: Holes turn pressure into speed
explainer.text: Nozzles trade pressure for speed: 0.14 bar inside a needle head throws jets out at 4.5 metres a second, and surface tension beads them into drops about 16 cm below. A rain shower has so much open area that an overhead tank can only make it dribble.

explainer.title: Litres, units and scalds
explainer.text: Water used is litres a minute times minutes: eight minutes at 9 L/min is 72 litres, five buckets, against one for a bucket bath. Heating it from 20 to 38 °C takes about 1.6 units of electricity. At 60 °C water burns skin in about five seconds, so store hot and mix down.

concepts.def: Outlet temperature = (hot flow × hot temperature + cold flow × cold temperature) ÷ total flow.
A fitting with a hot inlet, a cold inlet and valves that set how much of each flows into one outlet.
A small valve that sends the mixed water to the spout, the overhead shower or the hand shower.
A shower valve whose sliding spool keeps the hot and cold pressures equal, so the mix does not change when one supply dips.
A valve in which a wax capsule senses the mixed water and moves a shuttle to hold the temperature you set.
The height of the water surface above the outlet. Every metre gives about 0.1 bar of pressure.
A small hole that turns the pressure behind it into a fast jet; jet speed is about √(2 × pressure ÷ density).
The pull between water molecules at a surface, which pinches a thin jet into drops.
A burn from hot liquid. Adult skin is seriously burned in about 5 minutes at 49 °C and about 5 seconds at 60 °C.
